newsitem.title: UK: W.African crudes stable but face autumn decline.
newsitem.headline: W.African crudes stable but face autumn decline.

text.p: West African crude markets were balanced on Thursday with sellers happy to have cleared out most of August's barrels ahead of possible price falls, traders said.

Just a partial cargo of Qua Iboe was seen as still available from this month, aboard a VLCC part sold into the U.S. Gulf on Wednesday by a Swiss-based trader, and attention has firmly turned to trading September stock.
Another Qua Iboe traded from a U.S. refiner to a British major on Thursday.

With the freight thrown in the buyer saw the price as below 30 cents over Dated Brent but the seller, who fixed the vessel before recent rises in freight costs, pegged the sale of the cross-month loader at plus 35 cents.
Bonny Light was valued 40 to 45 cents above Dated, with second decade September cargoes on offer at plus 45 cents.
A French refiner sold a first decade BL into Spain on Monday at around +40 cents and a regular Nigerian grade seller moved BL barrels into the Senegal tender at the same price.
A second decade September combo Bonny medium/light was bought by a Chinese firm on Wednesday at around 20-22 for the first portion and 42-43 for the second, traders said.
First decade September barrels were reported scarce for some grades with no Bonny light and just one Medium/Light combo seen in the first 10 days of next month. But supply was good further out.
"There is some pressure from competing cargoes," said one seller. "There is more downside than upside as we go into September."

U.S. buying was steady but unspectacular, with more interest from Europe and Asia, he reported. Some 12 VLCCs have already been fixed to the Far East for September with two more of the large vessels likely to go the same way.
A second decade Forcados traded on Wednesday at a price heard to be 35 cents above Dated Brent and traders said the grade was still valued around that level.
Traders speculated that resumed Iraqi exports and the end of hefty U.S summer gasoline production may depress demand for West African barrels.
But others saw the effect of the extra sour barrels from Baghdad as muted.
"For Iraq, no would be a more honest answer than yes if you were to ask me if its having an effect," one trader said.
